text.p: Nagano Olympic officials denied on Thursday that Japanese environmental groups had threatened to attack next year's Winter Games if the men's downhill starts inside a national park.

"We haven't actually received any threats," said Makoto Kobayashi, director general of the Nagano organising committee. "But if we were to take the start up to 1,800 metres, we would receive threats."

Skiing's world body, which has pushed for a higher start, said on Wednesday that Nagano organisers had been warned that violent attacks would be made on the Games if the start was raised from 1,680 metres above sea level, which would put it into a national park.

"We have been told that there are threats, that if we impose a higher starting point that groups have informed the organising committee that they will attack the Games in a terrorist way," said Marc Hodler, president of the International Ski Federation (FIS) and a vice-president of the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
Nagano regional government officials said peaceful discussions were already underway with the groups.

"Nagano environmental groups are not terrorists and the Nagano prefectural government has been discussing the matter with them, so we don't think they are terrorists," said Mukio Kobayashi, director of the prefecture's Winter Olympics division.

The FIS wants to raise the start of the downhill in Hakuba, 50 km west of Nagano, to 1,800 metres above sea level to lengthen the run and include a spectacular jump. That would affect parts of the national park.
The world body has offered to run the race from the higher start point without the usual permanent structures.
But Nagano organisers have refused, citing environmental concerns.
Japanese environmental law forbids construction of permanent buildings in the park.

Gianfranco Kasper, secretary general of the FIS, said earlier at the Alpine skiing world championships in Italy that Nagano organisers had promised environmental groups when they first bid for the Games that the national parks would not be used.
Back-tracking over the downhill start would be considered a huge loss of face, he said.
Bernhard Russi, who designed the Nagano downhill course, said it barely encroached into the national park, mostly running alongside it rather than in it on the upper parts.
